title: The Tibetan traditions, closed
hookLine: four schools, the stages, mind training, the bardo

cards: A Tibetan practitioner finishes a session of practice. Maybe it was prostrations, maybe a mantra, maybe a quiet sit by a butter lamp. Before standing up, there's one more thing.

The hands come together, and a few lines are said, offering whatever good came from this practice to every living being, everywhere, without leaving anyone out. Then they get up and put the kettle on.
It takes less than a minute. And it's a good place to stand while looking back over this stretch of the path, because nearly everything in the Tibetan traditions leans toward that one gesture.

teach.b: The schools. Nyingma, the ancient one, tracing back to Padmasambhava and his hidden treasures. Kagyu, the line of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, with its long retreats and its songs.
Sakya, the school of the gray earth, teaching that the path and its fruit are joined. Gelug, the school of Tsongkhapa, with its great monasteries, its debates, its geshes, and now its geshemas.
Beside them, Jonang, the Rime movement that gathered teachings from many lineages, and Bon, Tibet's other tradition, with its own teachers and not a Buddhist school.
The stages: the lamrim, step by step, a precious human life, death, karma, refuge, all beings as our mothers, and finally calm and insight.
Mind training: Atisha's teaching, set out by Chekawa in seven points, sending and taking on the breath, bad circumstances as the path, the five strengths, two witnesses.

teach.h: THE BARDO AND THE CLEAR LIGHT.
teach.b: The bardo: death and the in-between, the clear light, the peaceful and wrathful visions recognized as the mind's own display, and a book read aloud beside the dying.

Around all of it: butter lamps, mani stones, thangkas painted by rule, the Kalachakra's sand swept away, tulkus returning, and the mountains from Ladakh to Mongolia. Different schools, different emphases.

But each, in its own words, sets this practice inside bodhicitta: the wish to wake up for the sake of all beings. That's why a session ends with the dedication. Whatever was done was never only for oneself.

how: In Tibetan Buddhist practice, a session traditionally begins by recalling bodhicitta, the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings, and ends by dedicating whatever merit came from it to all beings.

games.q: you've just finished a session of practice in the Tibetan way. the timer has gone off. what's the last step before you stand up?
o: offer whatever good came from it to all beings.
games.why: a session ends with the dedication: whatever good was done is offered to every being, without leaving anyone out.

practice: Wish someone you love well, then someone you barely know, a face from the street or the store, then someone difficult, and let the circle widen past every border to every being that breathes.

As the time closes, let whatever good came from this sit go out to all of them, the way the practitioner did before putting the kettle on. If you pray, you can use a dedication from your own tradition.

wordCard.voice: The Tibetan traditions. Four schools and their neighbors, the stages, mind training and the bardo, all held inside the wish to wake up for all beings. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: bodhi, awakening, and citta, mind or heart. The mind set on awakening for all beings.

carryVoice: Your line: for all beings. Tomorrow the path turns to other schools, starting in China. One stretch closed; the road goes on.
